caseStudies.title: Kubernetes Autoscaling for Transaction-Critical Services
caseStudies.summary: Validated and deployed Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) for a high-throughput service previously capped at static capacity, improving latency, errors, throughput, and CPU efficiency under production traffic.

engineeringPath.title: Baseline bottleneck
engineeringPath.detail: Equal minimum and maximum replica counts kept the service at fixed capacity, leaving no room for HPA to respond to demand.

engineeringPath.title: Autoscaling rollout
engineeringPath.detail: After urgent direction from a reliability engineering director, I tested over a weekend, then deployed and validated HPA using CPU first and memory later.

engineeringPath.title: Production comparison
engineeringPath.detail: Grafana averages over approximately 30-day baseline and comparison periods showed improved service behavior with a 50-100 pod range; exact dates are unconfirmed.

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: The service supported transaction-critical traffic with a fixed 20-pod deployment. HPA had not actually been enabled: its minimum and maximum replica counts were equal, so it could not change capacity in response to demand.

The failure mode was capacity exhaustion. When demand exceeded what those replicas could serve, the fixed ceiling prevented HPA from adding capacity; latency and errors were the service signals to examine alongside resource pressure.

sections.heading: Ownership and validation
paragraphs: A reliability engineering director asked for HPA to be enabled urgently. I tested over a weekend and concluded from those tests that enabling HPA could have avoided an outage. That is a test-informed counterfactual, not proof that a production outage was prevented.

I deployed and validated the change, using CPU as the initial scaling signal and adding memory later. I compared the baseline with subsequent production observations in Grafana, looking at latency, errors, request throughput, and average CPU together.

sections.heading: Decision and tradeoff
paragraphs: Keeping equal replica bounds makes capacity predictable, but leaves demand spikes dependent on manual capacity changes. Allowing HPA to vary replicas gives the service room to respond to resource pressure, at the cost of a larger and changing resource footprint. The production range moved to 50-100 pods rather than the previous fixed 20.

This was a bounded capacity decision: even dynamic scaling cannot add replicas beyond its maximum. Demand that exceeds the capacity available at that bound can still exhaust the service. Scaling adds headroom; it does not guarantee that every bottleneck or outage cause is removed.

sections.heading: Outcome
paragraphs: After rollout, mean latency moved from 121 ms to 72 ms (reported as 40% lower), weekly requests increased from 24.9M to 34.8M, and average CPU usage decreased 26%. The existing result also reports 89% fewer errors, but whether that measure is an error count or a normalized rate remains unconfirmed.
These are observed baseline-versus-comparison results alongside the capacity change. Request volume also changed, so the comparison does not isolate HPA as the sole cause of every improvement.

sections.heading: Evidence and limits
paragraphs: The measurements came from Grafana. I recall averages over approximately 30-day baseline and comparison periods; exact dates and the error measure's denominator are not confirmed. The weekly request figures describe throughput and should not be treated as those periods' total request counts.

I do not have confirmed stabilization settings, rollback checks, or team handoff details to share. This account therefore supports the testing, deployment, and observed comparison, but does not establish a complete recovery procedure or independently verified outage prevention.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: The first check is whether autoscaling has room to act: a configured HPA with equal bounds still leaves the service at fixed capacity. The next check is service behavior across multiple signals and changing traffic, with measurement limits stated alongside the results.

caseStudies.title: Production Order Reconciliation on GKE and Spanner
caseStudies.summary: Moved an internal daily order-reconciliation workflow from developer-run scripts to GKE, adapted it to Cloud Spanner, and followed through on production sequencing and queue failures.

engineeringPath.title: Move execution
engineeringPath.detail: Replace laptop execution and human credentials with a scheduled GKE workload.

engineeringPath.title: Adapt data access
engineeringPath.detail: Move from Cloud SQL to Spanner through an in-container PGAdapter and resolve cross-project access.

engineeringPath.title: Validate and repair
engineeringPath.detail: Progress from dry-run to writes, then investigate production sequencing and queue behavior.

sections.heading: Problem and ownership
paragraphs: Internal order reconciliation depended on developer-run scripts, database tunnels, and human GCP credentials. A recurring business workflow needed an operational execution path rather than a person's laptop. This system is separate from the public CDC case-count reconciliation application.

I productionized the workload with cdk8s Job/CronJob definitions, Terraform, and Spinnaker, implemented its workload identity and secret access, adapted the database integration, and addressed subsequent production defects. My ownership covered the workflow and its integration with dependent platforms.

sections.heading: Decisions and constraints
paragraphs: Moving execution to GKE changed both scheduling and the identity boundary. Workload Identity, least-privilege IAM, and Google Secret Manager/External Secrets replaced dependence on human credentials for this workflow.

The database target changed from Cloud SQL to Cloud Spanner mid-migration. The PGAdapter sidecar option was blocked, so I placed PGAdapter inside the application container. This preserved the required database compatibility path within the deployment constraint, at the cost of coupling adapter lifecycle to the application container.

Cross-project BigQuery IAM was another independent access boundary to resolve. A running container or successful Spanner connection alone could not establish that the complete reconciliation workflow had the required data access.

sections.heading: Validation, failure, and recovery
paragraphs: Production validation progressed through dry-run, single-order, and full-write execution. These stages separated basic access and comparison checks from the consequences of broader writes.

Production aftercare exposed different failure modes: a September sequencing race with the Elasticsearch gap report, followed by an October queue defect affecting batches larger than 100 items. I addressed those failures. Once items were released from initial and maxed_out states, normal processing reprocessed the approximately 2,200-item backlog. That is recovery evidence for this incident, not a guarantee about every future run.

sections.heading: Outcome and limits
paragraphs: The owner reports seven scheduled executions per week and estimates approximately 120 engineer-hours of recurring toil saved annually. The underlying per-run timing and annualization calculation have not been validated for this public account, so the estimate is not a measured productivity result.

The engineering lesson was to validate orchestration and queue boundaries alongside the database migration. For a future iteration, I would document representative batch sizes and dependency ordering as explicit acceptance checks. That is a proposed improvement, not a claim about tests that existed during the migration.

caseStudies.title: Booking Security and CI/CD Recovery
caseStudies.summary: Modernized release builds across approximately 15 booking services, directly remediating 10 and assisting with five, while restoring delivery paths blocked for roughly 11 months.
metrics: 66 unique critical/high CVE IDs removed from release builds

engineeringPath.title: Repair release inputs
engineeringPath.detail: Modernize frameworks, containers, and build behavior across the service estate.

engineeringPath.title: Validate changes
engineeringPath.detail: Use staged validation to distinguish security findings from delivery failures.

engineeringPath.title: Restore delivery
engineeringPath.detail: Recover release paths that had been blocked for roughly 11 months.

sections.heading: Problem and ownership
paragraphs: Security remediation was entangled with unhealthy delivery paths across approximately 15 booking services. Framework, container, and pipeline changes had to produce usable release builds; fixing a dependency finding alone would not restore a blocked release path.

I directly remediated 10 services and assisted with five others during September-October 2026. The work included Spring Boot and Quarkus modernization, container and build changes, code/SAST remediation, and pipeline recovery. The direct and assisted contributions reflect different levels of implementation ownership.

sections.heading: Decision and tradeoff
paragraphs: The alternative was to seek security exceptions. I chose to fix the underlying framework, container, and delivery problems so the release path could pass its gates through remediation. That choice does not mean an exception was requested or granted. Framework and container changes can remove vulnerable build inputs while also introducing compatibility failures, so validation had to cover both security and delivery.

The consequential tradeoff was the additional validation burden of changing several layers in an estate with already-blocked releases. Compatibility checks mattered alongside vulnerability results because the change had to recover delivery as well as improve the release inputs.

sections.heading: Verification and recovery
paragraphs: Changes went through staged validation, and PR scanning was added across seven applications. Release-build vulnerability results, code/SAST findings, and build-gate status provided distinct evidence. The failure mode to guard against was a cleaner scan paired with an application or pipeline that could no longer release.
Release paths blocked for roughly 11 months were restored. The supported security result concerns release builds; deployed-image remediation requires its own runtime evidence.

sections.heading: Outcome and lesson
paragraphs: The reported result was removal of 66 unique critical/high CVE IDs from release builds and remediation of 16 code/SAST findings, including four critical findings. The owner confirmed a final 100% build-gate pass across approximately 15 services, compared with the earlier reported 33%. Exact observation dates and a build-attempt denominator are unavailable; this is an owner-reported service-estate result.

My lesson was to keep security and delivery evidence separate while solving them together. In future reporting, I would retain per-service before/after build artifacts and exact observation windows to distinguish release-build remediation, gate recovery, and deployed-runtime status.

caseStudies.title: Evidence-Grounded AI-Assisted Payment Triage
caseStudies.summary: Led a four-person team across seven applications, implemented a little over half of the tool, and handed evidence-grounded payment triage to its receiving team for active use.
metrics: Active use by the receiving team

engineeringPath.title: Trace the system
engineeringPath.detail: Connect code and configuration with BigQuery and store telemetry.

engineeringPath.title: Ground findings
engineeringPath.detail: Use historical baselines, citations, coverage checks, and false-finding suppression.

engineeringPath.title: Transfer ownership
engineeringPath.detail: Validate with stakeholders, provide knowledge transfer, and hand off for active use.

sections.heading: Problem and ownership
paragraphs: Payment triage spanned seven applications and required investigation across code, configuration, BigQuery, and store telemetry. An explanation needed traceable evidence and enough coverage to avoid turning a plausible narrative into an unsupported finding.

The ask was to extend an existing skill/router. I led a four-person team, including myself, from design through stakeholder validation and handoff of that extension. I implemented a little over half of the tool; three other engineers contributed. I provided knowledge transfer and handoff to the operations and receiving teams. The receiving team now owns the tool and actively uses it.

sections.heading: Decision and tradeoff
paragraphs: Within that extension, the central design choice was to ground AI-assisted findings in code/config tracing, queried telemetry, historical baselines, and evidence citations. Coverage checks and false-finding suppression constrained what the tool should present. Making findings inspectable also made evidence collection and missing coverage part of the product's work.

Historical baselines provide context; they do not establish causality by themselves. Citations help a reviewer inspect support, but a citation is not proof that an interpretation is correct. The supported scope is cited evidence for human investigation. This operational triage tool is separate from the Jira-to-GKE hackathon delivery prototype.

sections.heading: Validation and failure modes
paragraphs: Stakeholder validation, coverage checks, and suppression of false findings were part of the work. Relevant failure modes include missing evidence, incomplete application coverage, a misleading baseline comparison, and a confident explanation that outruns its cited support. Those limits are why evidence quality belongs in the investigation flow rather than being an afterthought.

No reliable accuracy percentage or causal productivity measurement is available for this account. The evidence supports an evaluation approach and operational handoff, rather than numerical effectiveness. Examples below use placeholders to protect internal investigation data.

sections.heading: Outcome and lesson
paragraphs: The supported outcome is delivery through stakeholder validation, knowledge transfer, and handoff, followed by active use and ownership by the receiving team. That establishes operational adoption; it does not demonstrate that every suggestion is correct or that triage time fell by a measured amount.

My lesson was to treat implementation, evidence quality, and operational ownership as one delivery responsibility. A future evaluation should preserve representative reviewed cases, coverage gaps, and incorrect findings so usefulness can be measured. That is a recommendation, not a claim that a benchmark already exists.

caseStudies.title: JFrog OIDC and CI Credential Lifecycle
caseStudies.summary: Drove a move from shared Maven and Docker credentials to short-lived, job-scoped authentication across two teams and approximately 20 repositories.

engineeringPath.title: Identify exposure
engineeringPath.detail: Shared credentials and plaintext token output created a CI credential-lifecycle problem.

engineeringPath.title: Adapt authentication
engineeringPath.detail: Use short-lived job-scoped Maven/Docker authentication through JFrog OIDC.

engineeringPath.title: Verify adoption
engineeringPath.detail: Validate pipeline authentication in stages across the repository estate.

sections.heading: Problem and ownership
paragraphs: Shared Maven and Docker credentials crossed repository and job boundaries. The owner reported plaintext token output in CI logs across approximately 20 repositories, linked to more than 1,100 scanning findings. The finding count describes scanner results, not 1,100 distinct leaked secrets.

I drove JFrog OIDC adoption across two teams in October 2026, including CI pipeline adaptations for short-lived, job-scoped authentication. My role was to drive that cross-team change; participating repository work was shared.

sections.heading: Decision and trust boundary
paragraphs: The alternative I considered was a service account and password with custom masking. I chose OIDC and short-lived job-scoped tokens: masking addresses output handling, while job identity and temporary authentication also change how credentials are distributed and how long they remain usable. This made the identity-to-access boundary part of pipeline reliability.

The tradeoff is that artifact operations now depend on the OIDC exchange and its trust configuration. A failed exchange can block a build even when the application code is healthy. The public account omits private issuer, audience, subject, trust-policy, permission, and token-lifetime settings; the diagram illustrates the boundary without supplying deployable provider configuration.

sections.heading: Verification and recovery limits
paragraphs: The work included CI adaptations and staged verification of Maven/Docker authentication. Authentication and artifact-operation checks serve different purposes: accepting an identity is not, by itself, evidence that the job can complete its required artifact operation. Short-lived tokens also do not make printing tokens safe.

A future rollout should document recovery from a failed exchange without reintroducing shared secrets or logging token material. That is a recommended improvement; the historical recovery procedure is not documented here.

sections.heading: Outcome and lesson
paragraphs: The owner reports adoption across two teams and approximately 20 repositories, replacing shared credentials with short-lived, job-scoped tokens and resolving more than 1,100 findings tied to plaintext token output in CI logs. The scan tool, observation window, and deduplication method are unspecified; the finding count is not a distinct-secret count or a numerical measure of risk reduction.

I was the first to adopt this approach within my engineering organization and established it as the standard there. I reinforced that direction in a later engineer's migration PR review, explaining the implementation already in place and the rationale before approving. The reported implementation scope remains two teams and approximately 20 repositories; this is not a company-wide standard claim.

The lesson was to treat credential lifetime, job identity, pipeline usability, and logging behavior as related boundaries. A future evidence package should preserve redacted artifact-operation results and repeatable scan definitions so adoption and exposure reduction can be assessed independently.
